questions.question: Explain the heating effect of an electric current using particles. Give three appliances that use it, and explain how a fuse uses the heating effect to protect a circuit.
questions.expected_answer: As electrons drift through a conductor with resistance, they collide with the vibrating atoms and transfer energy to them; the atoms vibrate more strongly, so the temperature rises. More current or more resistance gives more heat (doubling the current gives four times the heat). Appliances: kettle, stove, toaster, iron, heater, geyser, filament bulb. A fuse is a thin wire of low melting point connected in series in the live side of the circuit; if the current exceeds the fuse's rating, the wire heats up enough to melt, breaking the circuit and stopping the current before the circuit's wires overheat and start a fire.

questions.question: Describe how to make an electromagnet, state three ways to increase its strength, and explain why soft iron is used as its core. Give two uses of electromagnets.
questions.expected_answer: Wind many turns of insulated copper wire around a soft iron nail or bolt and connect the ends to a cell through a switch; when current flows the nail becomes a magnet (picks up paper clips); when the current stops it loses its magnetism. Stronger with: more turns of wire, a larger current, a soft iron core. Soft iron magnetises strongly while current flows but loses almost all its magnetism when the current stops, so the electromagnet can be switched off (steel would stay magnetised). Uses: scrapyard cranes, electric bells, relays, circuit breakers, speakers, motors, security gate locks, MRI scanners.

questions.question: Define electrolysis, electrolyte and electrode. Describe the products of the electrolysis of acidified water and how to test them, and explain electroplating.
questions.expected_answer: Electrolysis is the decomposition of a substance by passing an electric current through it. An electrolyte is a liquid (solution or molten compound) that conducts electricity and is decomposed by it. Electrodes are the conducting rods or plates dipped into the electrolyte and connected to the source (anode positive, cathode negative). Acidified water: hydrogen forms at the negative electrode and oxygen at the positive electrode, with twice the volume of hydrogen as oxygen; hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint, oxygen relights a glowing splint. Electroplating: the object to be coated is made the negative electrode in a solution containing the coating metal; current deposits a thin layer of the metal (e.g. chrome, silver, gold) on it, for appearance and corrosion resistance.
